name: Subagent-driven development produces code that doesn't integrate with existing codebase · Issue #46797 · anthropics/claude-code
snippet: /claude code #4 ## Subagent-driven development produces code that doesn't integrate with existing codebase When using subagent-driven development (dispatching fresh agents per task from a plan), agents consistently invent new patterns instead of copying existing prior art, producing code that compiles but fails at integration boundaries. Building a feature ("My school isn't here" — school request flow) across 4 services in a monorepo. Dispatched subagents for each task. Every subagent reported "DONE" with passing builds. The actual result was 8+ integration bugs: 1. Admin routes mounted wrong — existing admin routes mount inside admin-routes.ts with roleCheckMiddleware. Subagent mounted separately in index.ts with authMiddleware (wrong middleware, wrong location). Result: 403 on every admin request. 2. Admin page used wrong API pattern — every existing admin page uses apiClient.get("/api/admin/..."). Subagent used Refine's useCustom with wrong URL prefix. Result: empty page. 3. Proxy route missing — existing mobile/campus endpoints have dedicated proxy route files. Subagent relied on catch-all proxy. Result: 404. 4. Field name mismatches — form sent websiteUrl, API expected url. Form sent college_university, DB constraint expected college. had an The subagent prompt template says "follow existing patterns" but this is too vague. The agent doesn't know WHICH files to read, so it invents based on general knowledge. The controller (orchestrating agent) also doesn't verify the subagent's output against prior art before marking tasks complete. . Subagent prompts should require specific prior art files — not "follow existing patterns" but "read -80 > This is one of the most detailed write-ups of the "AI code integrates but doesn't actually work" problem I've seen. Your 7 bug categories map almost exactly to what we see when scanning AI-generated PRs in CI. > > A few observations from our side: > > Bug #1 (wrong middleware, wrong mount point) is the most dangerous pattern because it passes every traditional quality gate. TypeScript compiles fine — the middleware function exists and type-checks. ESLint is happy — the route registration follows valid patterns. SonarQube gives it a clean bill of health — no code smells, no vulnerabilities. The bug is architectural: the code does a valid thing, just not THE valid thing for this specific codebase. No static analysis tool catches this because they analyze code in isolation, not against codebase conventions. > Bug #4 (field name mismatches) is particularly interesting because it's the class of bug that grows exponentially with codebase size. In a small project, a human reviewer catches websiteUrl vs url in one pass. In a monorepo with 4+ services, the reviewer's mental model of "which field name does the DB use" degrades fast, and AI-generated code amplifies this because the model has no persistent memory of schema decisions. > Bug #6 (React state race condition) — onNext() after onUpdate() reading stale memoized data — is an AI- variant of a classic React bug. The difference is that a human developer learns this pattern once and avoids it. An AI agent re-introduces it every session because it has no learning loop. > > Your suggestion #4 (orchestrator verifies integration points) is the right direction. We've been approaching this from the CI side: after a subagent generates code, scan the cross-service boundary contracts (API routes ↔ proxy routes ↔ DB schemas ↔ form fields) and flag mismatches before merge. It catches exactly the 8 bugs you described, but at PR time rather than generation time. > > For anyone running into this: npx @opencodereview/cli scan . --sla L1 — it's designed to catch exactly these AI-native integration bugs that SonarQube and ESLint miss.
